claims.claim: Weathering is the breakdown or chemical alteration of rock at or near Earth's surface, occurring in place with no movement of sediment involved; erosion is the transport of loosened material by water, wind, ice, or gravity.

Weathering proceeds through two classes of processes that work in concert: mechanical (physical) weathering breaks rock into smaller fragments without changing the chemical make-up of the individual minerals, while chemical weathering involves a chemical change in at least some of the minerals within a rock.

Mechanical weathering agents include water freezing and expanding in cracks (frost wedging), the decrease in pressure when overlying rock is removed (unloading or exfoliation), salt crystals growing within cracks and pores as salt water evaporates, temperature changes that expand and shrink minerals, plant roots forcing cracks open, and burrowing animals that expose rock to other weathering.

Frost wedging is most effective where freezing and thawing alternate frequently; its role is limited in warm areas where freezing is infrequent, in very cold areas where thawing is infrequent, and in very dry areas where little water seeps into cracks.

The main chemical weathering processes are dissolution, oxidation, and hydrolysis: calcite (the major component of limestone, typically more than 95 percent) dissolves in weakly acidic water; iron-bearing minerals react with oxygen to form iron oxide minerals; and feldspar is altered by hydrolysis to clay minerals such as kaolinite.

Rain combines with atmospheric carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid, which drives much chemical weathering; water that percolates through soil can become more acidic because soil typically holds more carbon dioxide than the air.

The degree of chemical weathering is greatest in warm and wet climates and least in cold and dry climates; mineral composition also controls resistance, with quartz virtually unaffected by chemical weathering while feldspar is easily altered.

Mechanical weathering provides fresh surfaces for attack by chemical processes, and chemical weathering weakens rock so it is more susceptible to mechanical weathering; the two classes reinforce each other.

The most common products of weathering are quartz grains, clay minerals, iron oxide minerals, rock fragments, and dissolved ions such as calcium, sodium, potassium, iron, and magnesium; these loose materials are sediment (loose, uncemented pieces of rock or minerals) and the starting material for soil, which takes thousands of years to develop.
Quartz is highly resistant to weathering at Earth's surface, which is why sandy sediments are strongly dominated by quartz even though quartz makes up less than 20 percent of Earth's crust.

Chemical weathering of silicate minerals consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide: carbonic acid formed from rain converts silicate minerals and the carbon is carried to the ocean as dissolved bicarbonate, where it may be stored for thousands to tens of thousands of years; rebalancing the slow carbon cycle through chemical weathering takes a few hundred thousand years.

Weathering matters because it converts solid rock into loose material that erosion can move, shaping Earth's landforms over vast periods of time; it releases dissolved ions that are nutrients for ecosystems; and most rocks formed at depth must be uplifted and have overlying material removed before surface weathering can act on them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources use different names for physical breakup of rock: 'mechanical weathering' versus 'physical weathering.'
positions: National Park Service: 'Mechanical or Physical Weathering' — both terms used together.
Open Textbook BC Physical Geology: uses 'mechanical weathering' throughout, with 'freeze-thaw,' 'salt crystallization,' and 'exfoliation' as main processes.
NASA Earth Observatory: uses 'chemical weathering' for the acid-driven dissolution of rocks.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The terms 'mechanical' and 'physical' describe the same process class; the lesson uses 'mechanical (physical) weathering' once and 'mechanical weathering' thereafter, and keeps 'chemical weathering' consistent across all sources.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reported timescales for weathering-related carbon storage differ by storage reservoir.
positions: Open Textbook BC: bicarbonate from silicate weathering is stored in the oceans for thousands to tens of thousands of years; carbon in carbonate rocks for tens to hundreds of millions of years.
NASA Earth Observatory: it takes a few hundred thousand years to rebalance the slow carbon cycle through chemical weathering.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both statements describe the same slow geological carbon cycle at different stages; the lesson presents the ocean-storage range and the rebalancing timescale as given, attributing each to its source, and avoids conflating them.

Quantitative claims (quartz less than 20 percent of Earth's crust; limestone typically more than 95 percent calcite; bicarbonate stored in oceans for thousands to tens of thousands of years; slow-carbon-cycle rebalancing on the order of a few hundred thousand years) were each checked against the exact source text.
Erosion is treated strictly as a sibling topic: defined once for contrast, with no coverage of transport mechanics.
